what_its_for: This medicine is a combination birth control pill used to prevent pregnancy. It contains two hormones — a progestin (desogestrel) and an estrogen (ethinyl estradiol) — that work together to stop ovulation (the release of an egg), thicken cervical mucus to block sperm, and change the lining of the uterus. Some forms may also be prescribed to help with acne or to regulate menstrual cycles.
how_to_take: Take one pill by mouth every day at the SAME TIME each day. It is very important to take it at the same time daily to get the best protection against pregnancy. You can take it with or without food. If it upsets your stomach, try taking it with a meal or at bedtime. Start your first pack on the first day of your period OR on the first Sunday after your period starts — follow your doctor's instructions. Use a backup method of birth control (like condoms) for the first 7 days if you are starting for the first time. Follow the arrows on the pill pack and take pills in order — do not skip or rearrange them. Some packs contain reminder pills (inactive/placebo pills) at the end — take these too to keep your habit of taking a pill every day.
dosing: The typical dose is one active pill taken by mouth once daily for 21 days, followed by 7 days of inactive (placebo) reminder pills, completing a 28-day cycle. Some packs (such as Kariva/Mircette) have a different schedule with low-dose estrogen pills in the last week — always follow your specific pack instructions. Do not take more than one pill per day. Your doctor will determine the right pack type and schedule for you.
missed_dose: If you miss 1 active pill: Take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next pill, take both missed and current pills at the same time. Continue the rest of the pack as normal. You likely do not need backup contraception. If you miss 2 active pills in a row in Week 1 or Week 2: Take 2 pills per day for 2 days in a row, then finish the pack normally. Use backup contraception (condoms) for the next 7 days. If you miss 2 active pills in a row in Week 3, or if you miss 3 or more active pills in a row at any time: Do not continue the current pack. Start a new pack immediately (Day 1 start) OR finish the current pack and start a new one after the last reminder pill. Use backup contraception for 7 days. Consider emergency contraception if you had unprotected sex in the past 5 days. If you miss a reminder (inactive) pill: Just throw it away and continue your pack — no backup is needed. When in doubt, use backup contraception and call your pharmacist or doctor.
storage: Store at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store in the bathroom medicine cabinet. Keep out of reach of children and pets. Do not use pills past the expiration date printed on the pack. Dispose of unused or expired pills safely — many pharmacies have medication take-back programs.
what_to_avoid: Do not smoke cigarettes while taking this medicine, especially if you are over 35 years old — smoking greatly increases the risk of serious blood clots, heart attack, and stroke. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice, as it may affect how the medication works in your body. Do not take herbal supplements such as St. John's Wort without talking to your doctor first, as it can make your birth control less effective. Certain medications can interact with this pill, including some antibiotics (rifampin), anti-seizure medications, and HIV medicines — always tell every doctor and pharmacist what you are taking. Avoid prolonged bed rest or long travel without moving your legs (blood clot risk). Limit alcohol and discuss any changes to your medications with your healthcare provider.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room RIGHT AWAY if you notice any of the warning signs remembered by the word ACHES: Abdominal pain (severe), Chest pain or shortness of breath, Headache (sudden, severe), Eye problems (blurred vision, loss of vision), Severe leg pain or swelling (possible blood clot). Also contact your doctor if you experience: Missed periods or signs of pregnancy, Jaundice (yellowing of the skin or eyes), Severe depression or mood changes, Breast lumps or unusual breast changes, High blood pressure, Severe allergic reaction (rash, hives, difficulty breathing, swelling of face or throat), Unusual vaginal bleeding, or Any new medications being prescribed by another doctor.
when_it_works: This birth control pill is most effective when taken correctly every day at the same time. When used perfectly, it is more than 99% effective at preventing pregnancy. With typical use (occasional missed or late pills), it is about 91% effective. It does NOT protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs) — use condoms for STI protection. If starting for the first time, use a backup contraceptive method for the first 7 days.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do NOT use this medicine if you are pregnant or think you may be pregnant. Stop taking it immediately and contact your doctor if you become pregnant. Breastfeeding: This medication is generally not recommended while breastfeeding, especially in the first 4–6 weeks after delivery, as estrogen may reduce milk supply. Talk to your doctor about progestin-only options if you are breastfeeding. Teenagers: This medication may be prescribed to adolescents who have begun menstruating; dosing is the same as adults. Smokers over age 35: This combination pill is generally NOT recommended — the risk of serious cardiovascular side effects is significantly increased. History of blood clots, stroke, heart disease, liver disease, certain cancers, migraines with aura, or uncontrolled high blood pressure: This medication may not be safe for you — discuss your full medical history with your doctor before starting. Older adults: This medication is typically discontinued at menopause and is not recommended for postmenopausal women.
